plain: The shared pipeline where a partner and AWS both write down the deals they're working.
real: If it isn't in ACE, AWS doesn't know it exists and nobody gets credit for it.

plain: Did the partner bring the deal, or help win one AWS already had?
real: Who gets the credit. This is why the meeting ran long.

plain: A negotiated price, transacted through AWS Marketplace instead of a normal contract.
real: The customer pays with money they already promised AWS. That's usually the whole reason it's on the table.

plain: A badge confirming AWS checked that a partner is genuinely good at one specific thing.
real: Months of paperwork and customer references. Also the thing that gets you into certain rooms.

plain: A partner's seller and an AWS seller working the same deal together.
real: Two comp plans pointed at one customer. Works beautifully, or not even slightly.

plain: Market Development Funds — money from AWS to pay for marketing partners do together with them.
real: It arrives with paperwork and a deadline, and it expires whether you spend it or not.

plain: The one sentence explaining why a customer should buy both things together.
real: Written by committee, which is why it's three sentences and commits to nothing. I have written several.

plain: We'll talk about it after this call.
real: Someone currently on this call should not hear the answer.

plain: One of the giant cloud providers — AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
real: Three companies whose roadmaps quietly set the agenda for everyone else's.

plain: The AWS portal where partners manage their relationship with AWS — deals, training, funding, listings.
real: Where the work is recorded, which is not always where the work happens.

plain: The storefront where customers buy software through their existing AWS account and bill.
real: Procurement's favorite shortcut, because the contract already exists.

plain: Software Composition Analysis — tooling that inventories the open-source components in an application and flags the ones with known vulnerabilities or license problems.
real: The thing that tells you which of the 900 libraries you didn't write is the one that'll ruin your quarter.

plain: The automated pipeline that builds, tests, and ships code every time a developer changes it.
real: The conveyor belt. Security tools either ride it or get ignored.

plain: Software Development Lifecycle — the whole path from writing code to running it in production.
real: Every team claims to have one. Ask where the exceptions get approved.

plain: Whether a company's cloud is configured safely — permissions, exposure, and misconfiguration.
real: Usually discovered to be worse than assumed, by about one order of magnitude.
